grammar.title: present simple and present continuous; state verbs; adverbs of frequency
grammar.explanation: We use the present simple for facts and things that are always or usually true. We use the present continuous for things happening now or around now. Some verbs describe states (feelings, thoughts), not actions, and we don't usually use them in the continuous form.
grammar.rule: present simple: facts, habits and routines → We study during the day and then we usually cook together in the evening. present continuous: temporary situations happening around now → I'm living with a few of the people on my course at the moment. state verbs: like, love, want, need, know, prefer, remember → stay in the present simple. adverbs of frequency: always, usually, often, sometimes, hardly ever, never – before the main verb but after be.
examples: I'm studying design and I love it!
I'm living with a few of the people on my course at the moment.
We study during the day and then we usually cook together in the evening.
My parents live back home in Poland.

rows.label: present simple
values: facts, habits and routines
My parents live back home in Poland.
When they come home, we always try to meet up.

rows.label: present continuous
values: things happening now or around now
I'm studying design and I love it!
I'm living with a few of the people on my course at the moment.

rows.label: state verbs
values: feelings and states – not usually continuous
I love it! (not: I’m loving it)

rows.label: adverbs of frequency
values: always / usually / often / sometimes / hardly ever / never
We always try to meet up when my parents come home.

grammar.title: verb patterns
grammar.explanation: Some verbs are followed by the to + infinitive form, and other verbs are followed by the -ing form. We can also use the -ing form as the subject of a sentence and after prepositions.
grammar.rule: verb + to + infinitive: decide, hope, need, want, agree, help, plan → After leaving school, I decided to do a plumbing course. verb + -ing: enjoy, finish, like, mind, spend time → Before studying to be a doctor, he worked as a volunteer. -ing form as subject: Working here is great! preposition + -ing form: She agreed to help before realising how hard it was.
examples: After leaving school, I decided to do a plumbing course.
She hopes to become a chef.
Working here is great – I love it!
Helping people is what Ridsdale does.

rows.label: verb + to + infinitive
values: decide to do • hope to become • need to speak
After leaving school, I decided to do a plumbing course.
She hopes to become a chef.

rows.label: verb + -ing
values: enjoy working • spend time learning | Working here is great – I love it!
Before studying to be a doctor, he worked as a volunteer in a hospital.

rows.label: -ing form as subject
values: Helping people is what Ridsdale does.

rows.label: preposition + -ing form
values: After leaving the food outside her home, she put up a sign.

grammar.title: modifiers
grammar.explanation: We use modifiers before adjectives and adverbs to make the meaning stronger or weaker. We can also use a bit before a comparative to talk about a small change, and a lot for a big change.
grammar.rule: weaker: quite / relatively / fairly + adjective → I would describe my lifestyle as quite normal. I guess my life is fairly comfortable. patterns: quite a … lifestyle / a bit more / a lot of.
examples: I would describe my lifestyle as quite normal.
My lifestyle is pretty normal.
I’m doing quite a lot of studying for university.
I want to travel a bit more.

rows.label: quite + adjective
values: I would describe my lifestyle as quite normal.

rows.label: pretty / relatively / fairly

I guess my life is fairly comfortable.

rows.label: quite a lot of + noun
values: I'm doing quite a lot of studying for university.

rows.label: a bit more / a lot more
values: I want to travel a bit more.

grammar.title: narrative tenses
grammar.explanation: When we tell a story, we use the past continuous to set the scene (background information), the past simple for the main events, and the past perfect to talk about an earlier event.
grammar.rule: past continuous: background information → They were sleeping on the floor. past simple: the main events → Suddenly, the train stopped in the middle of nowhere. past perfect: had + past participle for an earlier event → Jane woke up on the railway track. She had fallen off the train.
examples: They were sleeping on the floor when the train stopped suddenly.
I had never been on a jet ski before, so I was really excited.
When I found the right place, the driver had already left.

rows.label: past continuous
values: background information / to set the scene
They were sleeping on the floor.
She was getting very worried.

rows.label: past simple
values: the main events in the story
Suddenly, the train stopped in the middle of nowhere.
The driver left me on the beach.

rows.label: past perfect
values: an earlier event in the past
Jane woke up on the railway track. She had fallen off the train.
I couldn’t remember the exact beach where we had arranged to meet.

grammar.title: past simple and present perfect
grammar.explanation: The past simple describes an event that started and finished at a specific time in the past. The present perfect describes something that started in the past and continues, or is still important, now.
grammar.rule: past simple: an event that started and finished at a specific time in the past → In December 2019, researchers in Indonesia found a cave with paintings. present perfect: something that started in the past and continues, or is still important, now → People in the Middle East have told the story of Little Red Riding Hood for a thousand years. New technologies have brought exciting new ways to tell stories.
examples: People in the Middle East have told the story of Little Red Riding Hood for a thousand years.
New technologies have brought exciting new ways to tell stories.
In December 2019, researchers in Indonesia found a cave with paintings.

rows.label: past simple
values: started and finished at a specific time in the past
In December 2019, researchers in Indonesia found a cave with paintings.

rows.label: present perfect
values: started in the past and continues, or is still important, now
People in the Middle East have told the story of Little Red Riding Hood for a thousand years.

rows.label: present perfect of have
values: contracted form: I’ve, you’ve, they’ve
New technologies have brought exciting new ways to tell stories.

grammar.title: prepositions of time
grammar.explanation: We use before, until and during to talk about time in a narrative about a place or situation.
grammar.rule: until: the situation continues up to that time → The old way of life continued in Matera until the Italian government moved people out of the caves. before: earlier than that time → Before they moved into modern homes, families shared the caves with their animals. during: at the same time as a period → The changes happened during the 1950s.
examples: The old way of life continued in Matera until the Italian government moved people out of the caves.
Before they moved into modern homes, families shared the caves with their animals.
The changes happened during the 1950s.

rows.label: until
values: continues up to that time
The old way of life continued until the government moved people out.

rows.label: before
values: earlier than that time
Before they moved into modern homes, families shared the caves with their animals.

rows.label: during
values: at the same time as a period
The changes happened during the 1950s.

grammar.title: question forms
grammar.explanation: We can ask about the subject of a sentence (Who/What + verb) or about the object (Who/What + auxiliary + subject + verb). We also use question words like why, when, where, how and which with auxiliary verbs.
grammar.rule: subject question: no auxiliary → Who wrote the Sherlock Holmes books? (Tim Berners-Lee invented the web. → Who invented the World Wide Web?) object question: auxiliary + subject → What did Tim Berners-Lee invent? (Tim Berners-Lee invented the web. → What did he invent?) preposition at the end: What do you know a lot about?
examples: Who wrote the Sherlock Holmes books?
What did Tim Berners-Lee invent?
What do you know a lot about?

rows.label: subject question (no auxiliary)
values: Who wrote the Sherlock Holmes books?
Who invented the World Wide Web?

rows.label: object question (auxiliary)
values: What did Tim Berners-Lee invent?
Why do we have eyebrows?

rows.label: question ending in a preposition
values: What do you know a lot about?
What are you going to do later?

grammar.title: future plans and intentions
grammar.explanation: We use different forms to talk about the future. The present continuous is for arrangements we have already made. Going to is for plans and intentions. Will is for a decision made at the time of speaking. Might is for a plan we are not sure about.
grammar.rule: present continuous: a future arrangement → Next week we're looking at a house in a village. going to: future plans → They're going to travel around South America. will: a decision made at the time of speaking → We'll see if we can find somewhere nice, then we'll make our decision. might: a plan you are not sure about → I might get a job in a local restaurant.
examples: Next week we're looking at a house in a village.
They're going to travel around South America.
We'll see if we can find somewhere nice, then we'll make our decision.
I might get a job in a local restaurant.

rows.label: present continuous
values: a future arrangement

rows.label: going to
values: future plans
They're going to travel around South America.

rows.label: will
values: a decision made at the time of speaking
We'll see if we can find somewhere nice, then we'll make our decision.

rows.label: might
values: a plan which you are not sure about
I might get a job in a local restaurant.

grammar.title: indirect questions (polite inquiries)
grammar.explanation: Indirect questions are more polite than direct questions. In an indirect question, the word order changes: the subject comes before the verb, and we often use Can you tell me…?, Do you know…?, I’d like to know…?, Could you tell me…?
grammar.rule: word order: question word + subject + verb (no auxiliary after the question word) → Where is the swimming pool? → Can you tell me where the swimming pool is? (not: where is the swimming pool is) → direct: What time does the accommodation office close? → indirect: I'd like to know what time the accommodation office closes. yes/no questions use if/whether → Do I need a visa? → Do you know if I need a visa?
examples: Can you tell me where the swimming pool is?
I'd like to know what time the accommodation office closes.
Do you know if I need a visa?
Could you tell me if I can use the gym?

rows.label: Where is …?
values: Can you tell me where the swimming pool is?

rows.label: What time does …?
values: I’d like to know what time the accommodation office closes.

rows.label: Can I …?
values: Could you tell me if I can use the gym?

rows.label: Do I need …?
values: Do you know if I need a visa?

grammar.title: phrasal verbs
grammar.explanation: A phrasal verb is a verb + a small word (particle) with a special meaning. In some phrasal verbs, the object can go between the verb and the particle, or after the particle.
grammar.rule: separable phrasal verbs: I put on a song. = I put a song on. Inseparable phrasal verbs: My friends and I look out for each other. (not: look for each other out) phrasal verbs from the video: put on (a song), look out for (each other).
examples: Putting on a certain song can uplift you.
[It's important to] look out for each other.
I put on a song. / I put a song on.

rows.label: put on (separable)
values: to start playing (music)
Putting on a certain song can uplift you. → I put a song on.

rows.label: look out for (inseparable)
values: to take care of / protect
[It’s important to] look out for each other.

rows.label: find out
values: to discover
You are going to find out information about your partner’s answers.

rows.label: switch on / shut down
values: to start / stop a machine
I switch on my computer and begin work. At 4 p.m., I shut down my computer.

grammar.title: modals for rules and advice
grammar.explanation: Modal verbs change the meaning of the verb that follows. Some modals say something is necessary, some say it is not necessary, and some give advice.
grammar.rule: c = it is necessary. Have to / need to / must. a = it's a good idea: should. b = this isn't necessary: don't have to / needn't. d = don't do this, it isn't allowed or advised: mustn't.
examples: You need to set goals. You have to know what you want to achieve.
You don’t have to be more talented than everyone else, but you have to make more effort.
You must work really hard and you mustn’t give up.
You should be nice to people, but you needn’t work all the time.

values: must / have to / need to
It is necessary. You have no choice.
You must work really hard.
don't have to / needn't
This isn't necessary.
You needn't work all the time.
should / shouldn’t
a good idea / a bad idea
You should be nice to people.
mustn’t
Don't do this. It isn't allowed or advised.
You mustn't give up.

grammar.title: articles
grammar.explanation: Articles tell the listener or reader if we are talking about something new, something already known, or things in general.
grammar.rule: We use a/an the first time something is mentioned (new information) and with jobs. We use the when we know which person or thing we are talking about, and with superlatives. We use no article when we talk generally about people and things, and with most names of places.
examples: Who made the first flight?
He was an inventor called Alberto Santos Dumont.
The first flight happened in a field in North Carolina, USA, or in France.
The puzzle of who made the first flight remains one of the biggest questions in aeroplane history.

first mention (new information)
Books often say it was the Wright brothers.
a / an
jobs
He was an inventor.
the
known person or thing
The Brazilian’s flight was watched by hundreds of people.
the
superlatives
the biggest questions
no article
general people and things
Books about the history of flight
no article

grammar.title: How to… explain rules and procedures
grammar.explanation: When we explain rules and procedures, we present the information in a clear sequence with a clear structure, starting with more general information and then adding more details.
grammar.rule: Start with the aim: The aim of the game is to… Then say how it is organised: There are (six players). It is played on a field. Then the procedure: To start with… Then / Next… After that… . Then the rules: You score (shooting the ball into the goal). You can… You have to / must… You can't / mustn't… It lasts (one hour).
examples: That was the first time I have ever played floorball.
Let us know in the comments - are bowling, dance and fishing sports, or just hobbies?
The aim of the game is to score more goals than the other team.

values: how to win
The goal is to… / The aim of the game is to…
organisation and equipment
There are (six players). It is played on a field.
procedure
To start with… Then / Next… After that…
rules
You score (shooting the ball into the goal). You can… You have to / must… You can't / mustn't…

grammar.title: present perfect + superlative
grammar.explanation: We can use the present perfect + the superlative form of an adjective to talk about an experience related to our whole life.
grammar.rule: Subject + has/have + the superlative adjective + I've ever + past participle. Example: 'This is the worst… I've ever seen!'
examples: This is the worst… I've ever seen!
It's the worst hotel I've ever stayed in.
It's the longest journey I've been on!

values: This is the best + noun + I’ve ever + past participle
This is the best holiday I've ever had!
It's the worst + noun + I've ever + past participle
It's the worst hotel I've ever stayed in.
It's the longest + noun + I've ever + past participle
It's the longest journey I've been on!
